lesson.title: Berufe III: der Ingenieur, der Friseur, der Beruf, der Pilot, der Kellner
lesson.subtitle: where English borrowed hardest — and Beruf, vocation translated rather than inherited

hook.title: The French Shelf, the Cellar Man, and the Translated Word
hook.content: Three of today's five came off the French shelf — and English was in the same store. der Ingenieur is French ingénieur, built on Latin ingenium, 'what you are born with' — in- plus the root of gignere, 'to beget': inborn talent. English borrowed the same French word as engineer, and the Latin root had already crossed twice more: Old French engin meant 'cleverness, skill' before it ever meant a machine, which is why engine, engineer, ingenious and der Ingenieur are one Latin family. The engineer is literally the ingenious one. der Friseur is French friseur, 'the curler', from friser, 'to curl' — and English kept a curling word too: frizz, which dictionaries trace to the same French verb, though some hedge and call the resemblance a coincidence of sound. English even used friseur itself for a while, as a borrowed word for hairdresser. der Pilot took the long road: French pilote, on loan from Italian pilota — and English pilot is the same loan from the same chain, so this twin is nearly identical on both sides. German only splits the work differently: der Pilot flies, and the ship's guide gets a different word entirely (der Lotse). der Kellner looks like a loan but is homegrown compound logic: der Keller, taught back in Wohnen I — the twin of English cellar, both from Latin cellarium — plus the person ending. The Kellner was originally the cellar-master, the officer who kept the wine and the stores; English's exact match is cellarer, the monastery official in charge of the cellar. The waiter was the man of the cellar. And der Beruf is none of these: it is a translation. Literally 'what you are called to' (berufen, 'to call'), it got its modern meaning when Luther needed German for the New Testament's 'calling' — Greek klēsis — and reached for Beruf. English answered the same Greek with Latin: vocare, 'to call', gave vocation. So Beruf is vocation translated rather than inherited — a calque, not a cognate — and it is the word every -er job from the last two lessons hangs under.

footnotes.title: The -in Carries On
footnotes.content: German marks the women of these jobs with -in, exactly as in the last lesson: die Ingenieurin, die Friseurin, die Pilotin, die Kellnerin. Beruf itself takes no -in — it names the work, not the worker.

pattern.title: Asking Someone's Beruf
pattern.content: 1. The question: Was sind Sie von Beruf? (formal) or Was bist du von Beruf? (informal) — how German opens every job conversation. The answer stays bare: Ich bin Pilot. Ich bin Friseur — no article, as in the last two lessons. 2. The umbrella: Mein Beruf ist Ingenieur — der Beruf names the category, and every -er job from the last two lessons files under it: der Arzt, der Bäcker, der Verkäufer, der Student, der Fahrer, der Bauer, der Arbeiter. 3. The doer does the verb: Der Kellner bringt das Essen, der Pilot fliegt nach Spanien — zum Flughafen — der Ingenieur baut eine Brücke (the app's own name-word: Brücke and bridge are the same Proto-Germanic word), der Friseur spricht Französisch. 4. Plurals: the loans reshape — die Ingenieure, die Friseure, die Piloten (the Latin-style -en, like die Studenten) — while homegrown der Kellner stays bare: die Kellner, like die Fahrer.
pattern.linguist_note: Ingenieur and engineer are not inherited cognates but doublets: the same French word bought twice. English took engin from Old French by 1300 and built engineer on it; German waited until the sixteenth century and borrowed Ingenieur whole. When two languages shop in the same store for centuries, the aisles fill with doublets — and the older the purchase, the more it has bent: engine now means the machine, not the mind.

exercises.prompt: The borrowed jobs and the calling — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: What do you do for a living? (formal)
The waiter comes from the cellar
The pilot learns English, Spanish and Italian
matching_pairs.german: Der Pilot lernt Englisch, Spanisch und Italienisch

matching_pairs.english: The student has no profession yet
matching_pairs.german: Der Student hat noch keinen Beruf

matching_pairs.english: The hairdresser, the comb and the mirror
matching_pairs.german: Der Friseur, der Kamm und der Spiegel

exercises.target_answer: Der Ingenieur wohnt in Frankreich, Ich gehe zum Friseur, Mein Beruf ist Verkäufer, Was sind Sie von Beruf?, Der Pilot fliegt nach Spanien, Der Kellner bringt das Essen, Der Kellner kommt vom Keller, Der Friseur spricht Französisch, Der Pilot fliegt zur Schweiz, Der Pilot lernt Englisch, Spanisch und Italienisch, Der Student hat noch keinen Beruf, Der Friseur, der Kamm und der Spiegel
exercises.meaning: live in France, go to the hairdresser, your profession, asking the job, fly to Spain, bring the food
exercises.explanation: Five jobs, six frames. The jobs own their verbs: der Pilot fliegt (nach + the destination), der Kellner bringt — and bringen is English bring's own twin. Was sind Sie von Beruf? is the polite opener, answered with a bare profession: Ich bin Verkäufer — no article.

exercises.prompt: Three of today's jobs came through French (one by way of Italian first). One homegrown word is the abstract noun the others hang under. Which?
exercises.meaning: der Beruf ← berufen, 'to call': the homegrown umbrella, not a loan
exercises.explanation: Ingenieur and Friseur are straight French borrowings; Pilot is French that borrowed from Italian first. Kellner is homegrown too — but it names a person, the cellar-man. The word under all the others is der Beruf: Luther's translation of the biblical 'calling' (Greek klēsis). English answered the same Greek with Latin vocare — vocation. A calque, not a cognate.

exercises.prompt: der Kellner is der Keller + the person ending — the cellar-man, and Keller is the twin of English cellar (Latin cellarium). English kept the same job-title for the officer who ran a monastery's cellar. Which word is Kellner's twin?
exercises.explanation: cellarer is cellar + the person ending, from Latin cellarius — the monastery officer who kept the stores, exactly the Kellner's first job: der Keller + the person ending. cellar is the room, not the man; cellist is the instrument; sommelier is French's other steward-word, from a word for a pack-load — nothing to do with cellarium.

Bare profession after ist — no article, the frame from the last two lessons, now under the umbrella: Mein Beruf ist Ingenieur. The bank keeps two more jobs to prove the frame scales: Mein Beruf ist Friseur; Mein Beruf ist Kellner.

fliegt is fliegen in the third person — and fliegen, flog, geflogen is the same ablaut row as fly, flew, flown. nach marks the destination, as it did with Spanien in the first exercise. The bank's extra chips stay in the pilot's world: der Flughafen he leaves from, der Ingenieur whose Brücke he flies over, der Kaffee he hopes is waiting.

summary.outcome: Ask what someone does for a living, name the loan jobs, file every -er job under der Beruf, and tell why the waiter was once the cellar-man.

use_example.german: Was sind Sie von Beruf? — Ich bin Pilot.
use_example.english: What do you do for a living? — I am a pilot.

summary.takeaway: Ingenieur and engineer are the same French word (Latin ingenium, the mind's engine); Friseur is the curler; Pilot is the French-Italian loan English shares; Kellner is the man of the Keller, twin of cellar; Beruf is vocation translated, not inherited.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: when der Beruf goes home for the day — die Musik, der Sport, das Lied, tanzen, malen.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Berufe III: der Ingenieur, der Friseur, der Beruf, der Pilot, der Kellner (The pilot flies to France):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Pilot fliegt nach Frankreich" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Berufe III: der Ingenieur, der Friseur, der Beruf, der Pilot, der Kellner without relying on short-term echo.

ingenieur.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French ingénieur — the same French loan as English engineer. [wiktionary]

friseur.etymology_derivation: A French-style formation from frisieren; no standard English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

beruf.etymology_derivation: Literally the calling, deverbal of berufen (to call) - the same idea as English vocation (Latin vocare, to call), though the words are unrelated. [wiktionary]

pilot.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1500 from Italian pilota, partly via French pilote - the same Italian word that gave English pilot. [wiktionary][etymonline]

kellner.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin cellenarius (cellarer), from Late Latin cellarium - the pantry word that also gave German Keller and English cellar. [wiktionary][etymonline]

braun.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *brūn — English brown is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

schweiz.etymology_derivation: die Schweiz is named after Schwyz, the canton the country takes its name from. [wiktionary]

englisch.etymology_derivation: From England plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the page itself names English English as the cognate, so this is the same word. [wiktionary]

spanisch.etymology_derivation: Spanien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Spanish. [wiktionary]

italienisch.etymology_derivation: Italien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Italian. [wiktionary]

bäcker.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of backen (bake) + -er, Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz — the direct twin of English baker. [wiktionary]

verkäufer.context_phrase: Der Verkäufer zeigt mir die Schuhe.
verkäufer.context_translation: The salesman shows me the shoes.
verkäufer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of verkaufen (sell, the kaufen/cheap family); English uses a different root for seller. [wiktionary]

student.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin studēns — a Latin loan both languages borrowed alike. [wiktionary]

fahrer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of fahren (to fare/drive) + -er — the fare family again. [wiktionary]

pass.etymology_derivation: From Old French pas, from Latin passus (step); the passport sense is a shortening of French passeport, the same source English used. [wiktionary]

gepäck.context_phrase: Mein Gepäck ist noch nicht da.
gepäck.context_translation: My luggage is not here yet.
gepäck.etymology_derivation: A collective of Pack (bundle) — the Low German packing word English also took as pack. [wiktionary]

keller.context_translation: The bicycles are standing in the basement.
keller.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kellari, from West Germanic kellari, an early loan of Late Latin cellarium; English cellar is the same Latin word through Old French. [wiktionary]

kamm.context_phrase: Ich brauche einen Kamm für die Haare.
kamm.context_translation: I need a comb for my hair.
kamm.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kambaz, from PIE gombhos, meaning tooth; English comb is a direct cognate, and both keep the old idea that a comb is full of teeth. [wiktionary]

spiegel.context_phrase: Der Spiegel hängt an der Wand.
spiegel.context_translation: The mirror hangs on the wall.
spiegel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spēgl, an early adoption of Latin speculum; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

frankreich.etymology_derivation: Franke "Frank" + Reich "realm" — realm of the Franks. [wiktionary]

flughafen.etymology_derivation: Flug (flight) + Hafen (port) — the flight-port; see der Fernseher-style calques. [wiktionary]

französisch.etymology_derivation: From Old French francois plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; both trace back to the Franks, whence also English frank. [wiktionary]

brücke.context_phrase: Die alte Brücke ist aus Stein.
brücke.context_translation: The old bridge is made of stone.
brücke.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *bruggju — the page lists English bridge as the cognate; German keeps the hard k where English softened to dg. [wiktionary]

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).
